cards.title: The Three Fallacies of Innovation Data
cards.summary: Growing companies drift from customer jobs because operators fall for three data traps: active-vs-passive data, surface growth, and conforming data.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a once jobs-focused ecommerce brand now chases product lines, channel metrics or exec pet projects instead of customer progress.
steps: Name the three fallacies explicitly in a leadership review so the team has shared language: (1) Active versus Passive Data — after launch, spreadsheets about sales, customers, assets and competitors crowd out the messy context-of-struggle data that revealed the job. (2) Surface Growth — sunk investment in customer relationships creates incentive to sell more products to existing customers or solve more jobs, rather than solving the core job better. (3) Conforming Data — data gets shaped to support the preexisting business model and the functional agenda of whoever presents it.

For each, ask what evidence would show you are in it: are decisions driven mainly by product-mix and channel dashboards? Is the catalog or SKU count growing faster than clarity about who each item is for? Does each function bring data that conveniently supports its own plan?
Treat awareness as only the first step — chronic exposure requires ongoing vigilance, a named owner and intervention, not a one-off workshop.
Keep the reference to Levitt/Drucker: customers buy the quarter-inch hole, not the drill; product-defined self-image is the root cause of the drift.
caveats: The fallacies describe tendencies in the authors' research and experience, not a measured law; treat as diagnostic lenses.
The V8 case (sales quadrupled in under a year after re-framing against vegetables) is a single anecdote, not a benchmark or promise.

Reorganizations are usually impractical; the authors recommend embedding jobs focus in processes, metrics and culture over time rather than large reorgs. A cited 2010 Bain study of 57 major reorganizations found fewer than one-third produced meaningful performance improvement.

cards.title: Passive Data Needs Active Management
cards.summary: The context-rich signal that reveals a job has no voice, structure or champion, so leaders must deliberately give it a standing role in decisions.
cards.use_when: Setting up research cadence and decision rights so customer-job evidence survives contact with the operating dashboard.
steps: Recognize that passive data — the unfiltered context of customers' struggles, frustrations, workarounds and undesirable tradeoffs — is always present but never loud, and has no champion or agenda.

Because the job itself does not change much while operations data changes constantly, managers naturally respond to the loud operations signal; install a counterweight rather than relying on good intentions.
Assign a specific person or forum to own and present job evidence in innovation and investment decisions, so it competes on equal footing with product, sales and finance data.

In early-stage or new-opportunity work, act as a puzzle solver rather than a number cruncher: seek out nonconsumption and workarounds, assemble the narrative of the struggle, and relentlessly ask why.
Design processes to be flexible so the way you solve the job can adapt as circumstances change, instead of freezing one interpretation of the job into policy.
caveats: Passive data is qualitative and context-dependent; it is directionally helpful, not objective reality, and will not survive being reduced to a single KPI.
The authors' argument that no customer has a job called 'I need to spend a couple of hours at the store' is an assertion about retail, not a general law.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Surface Growth vs. Solving the Core Job Better
cards.summary: Copying competitors' products or piling new jobs onto the same customers grows revenue on paper while diluting the job that won the customer.
cards.use_when: Evaluating catalog expansion, brand extension, line extensions or acquisition of adjacent product lines before committing.
steps: Flag surface growth when the logic for a new product is 'our existing customers could also buy this' or 'competitors sell it, so we can too' rather than 'this solves the same job better.'

Consider the DeWalt pattern: a brand built on a stellar radial arm saw expanded into aisles of imitative drills and clamps, often outsourced for cheap production; the authors argue that stealing revenue with lower-quality imitations is not a growth plan to count on.

Consider the New York Times pattern: serving many jobs for the same readers (unwind, stay current, feel informed, fill time productively) exposes you to a focused competitor for each job — The Economist for weekly briefing, TV for unwinding, free commuter papers for filling time.
Keep the job spec as the screen for expansion: if the new offer cannot be tied to the core job, expect customer confusion about what the brand is for and firing of the wrong product.
Watch the 'sweat the assets' pressure from sunk investment in production, IP and talent, especially under short-horizon shareholders — it is the mechanism that converts small add-ons into drift.
caveats: This does not forbid any expansion; it warns that expansion without a job rationale confuses customers and invites focused disrupters.

The V8 line proliferation (Spicy Hot, Lemon, Picante, Roasted Chicken, Low-sodium, Organic, Splash, V-Fusion + Tea) is the authors' illustrative example of lost clarity, not a measured failure of any specific flavor.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Conforming Data: Why You Miss the Obvious
cards.summary: Each function brings data that supports its own incentives, and decision 'leaps' are often pre-skewed before the meeting starts.
cards.use_when: Running innovation, range or investment reviews where sales, marketing, product and finance all present supporting numbers.
steps: Expect predictable positions: sales claims to know customer needs from constant contact; marketing proposes brand-leverage variants (new versions, flavors, colors, offers); product/R&D pushes features and technology; the business head pushes whatever can hit the P&L this year. Each arrives with carefully constructed supporting data.
Accept that none of these views is wrong but none is objective, and none models the customer's job — so a decision cannot be made simply by weighing the decks.

Counteract confirmation bias with Nate Silver's point: prediction failures cluster where we focus on signals that tell the story we want, not the story that is; and Holmes's 'nothing is more deceptive than the obvious fact.'

Apply Gerald Zaltman's cautions: decisions often 'happen' rather than get made, and a common error is treating facts as insights and leaping from data straight to action — data should fuel imaginative insight, not prove a point.
Before the meeting, publicly ask what data should be created and which dimensions should be ignored; senior leaders should invest as much in designing measurement as in analyzing it.
If a decision looks like A-vs-B, audit the layers beneath it to see whether the data was already skewed toward A before the leader entered.
caveats: This is a critique of decision process, not a claim that quantitative data is worthless — the point is that all data is man-made and embeds choices.
Psychological dissonance-avoidance is offered as an explanation of the pattern, not a tested organizational law.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: All Data Is Made by Someone with an Agenda
cards.summary: Numerical precision hides judgment: financials, big-data models and surveys all embed human choices about what to count.
cards.use_when: Choosing or defending a data source for a positioning or product decision, or when a team treats dashboards as ground truth.
steps: Stop privileging quantitative over qualitative on the assumption that only numbers are objective; both are abstractions from a more complex reality, and qualitative subjectivity is at least visible while numeric bias hides behind precision.

Recognize that financial-statement revenues, costs and profits result from estimation, negotiation, debate and politics in allocating overhead — Johnson and Kaplan showed these can grossly misstate true cost and profit.

Use the Google Flu Trends parable as the cautionary case: 50 million search terms matched against 1,152 data points overestimated US flu cases for more than two years; the Science analysis blamed 'algorithmic dynamics' and 'big data hubris' rooted in engineers' modeling choices. Just because search behavior can be computed does not make it valid data.
Ask who created this data, what they chose to collect, organize and present, and what meaning they inferred — data carries the agenda of its creator whether intended or not.
Keep Tom Monahan's 'Museum of False Precision' joke as a cultural shorthand for humility about dashboards.
caveats: The authors still call search-trend data directionally helpful; the objection is to treating it as objective reality, not to using it at all.
The Bobby Kennedy GNP passage and the author's son's HBS section-leader story are illustrative arguments about unmeasured value, not research findings.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Jobs as the Unit of Analysis: TurboTax's Shift from Interview to Done
cards.summary: Reframing from the product's internal component to the customer's desired outcome unlocks creativity and a clearer roadmap.
cards.use_when: When feature requests and backlog items pile up but no one can say which ones matter, or a core product step has become the optimization target itself.
steps: Notice the flawed unit of analysis: Intuit's team spent years perfecting the TurboTax interview (questions, data entry, accuracy) because that was the visible product surface.
Recognize that customers were not hiring TurboTax to get a better interview — they hired it to get their taxes done, and did not want to answer questions or enter data at all.

Reframe the goal to 'taxes are done' and let that drive the roadmap, even if the full vision takes a decade; Sasan Goodarzi's reframing produced an immediate burst of creativity once the team focused on the job.
Pursue interim steps that reduce work for the customer, not just polish the existing flow: with permission, prefill data such as W-2 information pulled from payroll providers like ADP.

Use the 2015 experiment as the pattern: preloading data in just one 'chapter' of the questionnaire (there are roughly four to forty chapters depending on the taxpayer) produced a noticeable uptick in interview completion, even though customers still had to correct some auto-filled data.
Treat survey wish lists (customers asking for 150 features) as unusable without a job definition: Scott Cook's view is that feature requests without a job are 'like navigating without a compass.'
caveats: The chapter-prefill result is a company experiment, not a published benchmark or guaranteed lift.
Full 'no interview' TurboTax is described as years away; interim progress is still meaningful but incomplete.
Scott Cook frames the challenge of sustaining focus as an open question — 'the sixty-four-billion-dollar question' — rather than a solved management problem.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Four Organizational Benefits of a Jobs Focus
cards.summary: Jobs clarity pays off in decision autonomy, resource allocation, culture and measurement — four distinct levers, not one vague morale boost.
cards.use_when: Making the internal business case for adopting jobs-based language, or auditing which of the four benefits is actually missing.
steps: Distributed decision making with clarity of purpose: when the job is understood, employees at all levels can make good jobs-aligned decisions autonomously and innovate without escalation.
Align resources against what matters most — and free resources from what does not; jobs clarity makes it easier to decide what does and does not belong in the offer.
Inspire people and unify culture around what customers care about most, so individual workstreams have evident meaning.
Measure what matters most: customer progress, employee contributions and incentives — not only product and channel metrics.

Use the job as 'commander's intent': a well-articulated job spec lets people balance necessary tradeoffs without being told each time what to prioritize (what is most important, what cannot be compromised, what the ultimate goal is, what their role is).
Expect this to build over time through shared learning; a culture that forms around the job becomes self-managing and does not require rule enforcement.
caveats: The four categories are drawn from CEOs the authors interviewed, not from controlled study.
The authors acknowledge unanswered questions about how to keep teams consistently rallying around a hard goal; treat this as direction, not a complete operating system.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Why Mission Statements Fail as Daily Guides
cards.summary: Generic mission statements inspire but cannot arbitrate daily tradeoffs; a specific job spec can.
cards.use_when: When a company has a mission or purpose statement that nobody can translate into product, service or merchandising decisions.
steps: Test the mission against daily use: examples like 'to help all people live healthy lives,' 'to be the most respected financial services firm in the world' or 'to realize the tremendous potential of the railway' are too high-level and generic to guide action, decision making and innovation.

Keep the mission if it works as a theme, but do not mistake it for an operating guide — the authors compare mission statements to life themes like 'I want to be a good parent,' useful but not actionable alone.

Nest a job under the mission. Unilever's Lifebuoy kept the mission of helping children in emerging markets live to five, then specified the job: make handwashing actually happen in real circumstances.

Anchor the job in circumstances and thresholds: experts say thirty seconds of vigorous washing with soap and hot water eliminates germs, yet most people wash about seven seconds and rarely more than fifteen, and children hurry more; in India nearly 400,000 children under five died from diarrheal disease in a year at the time described — over a thousand deaths a day.

Design to the real circumstance, not the ideal one: color-changing soap signals when ten seconds is reached (sufficient with Unilever's special formula) and makes it more fun for children to stay with it.
Generalize the lesson: the more precisely you understand the job, the more it can connect internally and the more innovation it can drive.
caveats: The Lifebuoy outcome is a company success story (one of the fastest-growing brands in the period described), not a controlled trial of the job-framing method.
Health behavior thresholds cited are as reported by the source; do not restate them as current medical guidance outside that context.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Two-Sided Compass: Using the Job to Decide What Not to Do
cards.summary: A clear job definition narrows options productively — deciding what does not belong as much as what does — and speeds crisis decisions.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing a service, feature or benefit roadmap where everything looks technically feasible and marketable.
steps: Shift focus from cool 'brochure ware' features to benefits aligned with the job; OnStar's clarity that customers hired it for peace of mind while driving let the team judge what belonged in the suite and what did not.
Accept that narrowing feels limiting but provides clarity: less time and energy is spent evaluating options, and technical priorities become easier to rank.

Use the job as a compass heading for unanticipated events: when Hurricanes Katrina and Rita hit the Gulf Coast less than a month apart in 2005, OnStar's call center was flooded with panicked callers, some of whom were told mid-evacuation that real-time directions required a plan upgrade.

Decide by the job, not by the upsell opportunity: by Rita's approach the team treated these as regional crisis events, and the employee responsible for that business simply decided to give anyone calling from a crisis area all OnStar services immediately without requiring an upgrade — the founding CEO describes it as about a fifteen-second conversation.

Execute even when systems resist: OnStar had to build workarounds ('duct tape and Velcro') to detect calls from a crisis region and route them to a specialized team with evacuation routes and weather information.
Embed this in the team's instincts: when something clearly intersects the compass heading, people get on it rather than resisting 'one more thing'; clarity of purpose motivates the best work.
caveats: The fifteen-second decision was fast, but implementation was not — the source distinguishes deciding from executing and acknowledges imperfect workarounds.
OnStar's founding-CEO account is a single-company narrative, not evidence that any organization can replicate the autonomy.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Make Jobs the Common Language Across Functions
cards.summary: A one-syllable phrase gives marketing, engineering, sales and service a shared reference point instead of talking past each other.
cards.use_when: Cross-functional planning sessions where each department optimizes its own metrics and meetings end without alignment.
steps: Adopt jobs language as the integration layer: marketers, engineers, salespeople and customer service can communicate through it rather than through their own functional models.
Keep the articulation simple and unengineered — Jobs To Be Done is one-syllable words, and, as Mercer's Jacques Goulet puts it, its simplicity is what focuses the mind.
Expect strategy to be formed in everyday choices about resources, processes and priorities; jobs clarity is the 'intuitive playbook' employees draw on when no instruction exists.
Note the caveat that getting jobs-based goals right is hard — jobs are complex and nuanced and require deep understanding of the progress a customer is trying to make.
When done well, expect a productivity effect: clarity lets a much greater share of human capital be deployed with the right balance of autonomy and alignment.
caveats: The claimed productivity impact is a leadership observation from the authors' interviews, not a measured effect size.
Simple language does not mean simple analysis; the difficulty of defining jobs accurately is stated explicitly.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Leader Questions to Audit Jobs-Centeredness
cards.summary: A reusable question set reveals whether the customer's job is genuinely guiding product, marketing, service and investment decisions.
cards.use_when: Running a quarterly strategy or innovation review, or onboarding a new functional leader, to test alignment around customer progress.
steps: Ask whether the customer's job guides all critical decisions in product development, marketing and customer service.
Ask whether the functions that shape the customer experience (product, service, marketing, sales, after-sale service) support nailing the job in a coordinated way or are in conflict.
Ask what new processes could ensure more integrated delivery of the experiences the job requires.
Ask which elements of the end-to-end experience are most critical to perfectly solving the job, and what metrics would track performance against those elements.
Ask how people would characterize the fundamental business: in terms of solving an important job in customers' lives, or in terms of the products and services offered.

Ask what data drives innovation and investment decisions and how closely it connects to customers' jobs; probe specifically for surface growth — extra products sold to existing customers without understanding the progress customers seek.
Ask what mechanisms ensure the data presented reveals what you need to see rather than what is comfortable to believe, and how the job has a voice in resource allocation.

Follow the authors' process advice rather than restructuring: carefully set up and integrate the right processes, measure the right things, and over time embed jobs centricity in culture, building in flexibility so solutions can adapt.
caveats: These are the authors' diagnostic prompts, not a validated assessment instrument.
The process-over-reorg recommendation is a general argument; it does not guarantee culture change without sustained leadership attention.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Levitt and Drucker: The Drill-vs-Hole Disconnect
cards.summary: Customers buy solutions to problems, yet company behavior usually reveals a product-defined self-image — the core gap Jobs Theory addresses.
cards.use_when: Teaching or re-anchoring a team on customer-centric framing before writing positioning, roadmaps or campaign briefs.
steps: State the premise plainly: people do not want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole; customers do not want products, they want solutions to their problems. The authors attribute the popularization to Ted Levitt, who in The Marketing Imagination credited Leo McGinneva.
Use Drucker's parallel warning that the customer rarely buys what the company thinks it is selling to frame the company-customer disconnect.

Expect company drift after success: most successful organizations were de facto founded on an identified job, but after launch the job gets lost and the company defines itself by products — this is a common pattern even among the best companies.

Apply the railroad lesson: the railroad industry declined not because transportation demand fell (it grew) but because cars, trucks, planes and telephones did the job better; as Levitt wrote in 1960, railroads assumed they were in the railroad business rather than the transportation business.

Note the self-defining market frame: no customer has a job called 'I need to spend a couple of hours going to the store,' so brick-and-mortar-organized retailers tend to play defense; OpenTable, Salesforce.com, Airbnb, craigslist and IKEA are cited as businesses organized around a distinct job with minimal competition.

For startups, treat the founder's own struggle as a research asset: the Netflix origin story began with an entrepreneur in a circumstance with no clear solution saying 'I'm going to fix this,' collapsing the distance between innovator and customer job.
caveats: The 'no customer job to go to the store' claim is illustrative of the authors' framework, not an empirical finding about all retail.
The listed successes are examples chosen to illustrate job-centered organizing; their outcomes are not attributed to this framework alone.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx
